lesson.readTheTable.title: Reading the Periodic Table
lesson.readTheTable.summary: Periods run across, groups run down. Learn what each axis controls before you memorise a single number.
lesson.readTheTable.q1: What increases as you move left to right across a period?
lesson.readTheTable.q2: Elements in the same group share what property?
lesson.readTheTable.q3: Where are the lanthanides and actinides normally drawn?
lesson.readTheTable.e1: Atomic number increases by one each step because you are adding one proton. Everything else (radius shrinks, electronegativity rises) follows from that.
lesson.readTheTable.e2: A group is defined by valence electron count, which is why the alkali metals (1) and the halogens (7) each behave alike.
lesson.readTheTable.e3: They are the f-block, pulled out below the table to keep columns 3–12 readable. They still belong to periods 6 and 7.
lesson.atomicStructure.title: Atomic Structure
lesson.atomicStructure.summary: Protons decide the element, neutrons make the isotope, electrons make the ion. Three particles, three jobs.
lesson.atomicStructure.q1: Which particle determines the identity of an element?
lesson.atomicStructure.q2: Two atoms of the same element with different neutron counts are called…
lesson.atomicStructure.q3: A sodium atom that loses one electron becomes…
lesson.atomicStructure.e1: Change the protons and you change the element entirely. Iron with 25 protons is manganese; with 27 it is cobalt.
lesson.atomicStructure.e2: Isotopes share a proton count and differ in mass number. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon; carbon-14 is radioactive.
lesson.atomicStructure.e3: Losing an electron leaves one more proton than electron, so the charge is +1. The element is still sodium.
lesson.electronConfig.title: Electron Configuration
lesson.electronConfig.summary: Fill sub-shells in energy order, then read the configuration back. Aufbau, Hund and the noble-gas shorthand.
lesson.electronConfig.q1: In which order does the Aufbau principle fill sub-shells?
lesson.electronConfig.q2: How many electrons fit in a single p sub-shell?
lesson.electronConfig.e1: Sub-shells fill by increasing n + l, so 4s (n+l = 4) comes before 3d (n+l = 5). That is why potassium is [Ar] 4s¹, not [Ar] 3d¹.
lesson.electronConfig.e2: Each sub-shell holds 2(2ℓ+1) electrons: s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14.
lesson.electronConfig.e3: Noble-gas shorthand substitutes the full configuration of a noble gas. [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² is iron: 18 + 6 + 2 = 26 electrons.
lesson.trends.title: Periodic Trends
lesson.trends.summary: Radius, electronegativity and ionisation energy all follow from one thing: how tightly the nucleus holds its electrons.
lesson.trends.q2: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
lesson.trends.q3: Why is the first ionization energy of sodium much lower than that of neon?
lesson.trends.e1: Down a group you add shells, so the atom is physically bigger. Across a period increasing nuclear charge pulls the same shell inward.
lesson.trends.e2: Fluorine is 3.98 on the Pauling scale — the highest of any element, and it pulls hardest on bonding electrons.
lesson.trends.e3: Sodium’s 3s¹ electron is shielded and far from the nucleus. Neon’s 2p⁶ are close in and tightly held, so removing one costs far more energy.
lesson.ions.title: Ions and Polyatomic Ions
lesson.ions.summary: Cations, anions and polyatomic ions — how charges arise and what each one does in solution.
lesson.ions.q1: A monatomic ion with a 2− charge has how many more electrons than protons?
lesson.ions.q2: Which of these is a polyatomic ion?
lesson.ions.q3: What charge does an oxide ion carry?
lesson.ions.e1: A negative charge means the ion has gained electrons — 2− means two extra electrons.
lesson.ions.e2: Sulfate contains four atoms bonded together. Monatomic ions like Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are a single atom each.
lesson.ions.e3: Oxygen is in group 16 with six valence electrons and gains two to reach an octet, giving O²⁻.
lesson.bonding.title: Chemical Bonding
lesson.bonding.summary: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, and the evidence that tells them apart.
lesson.bonding.q2: A metal like iron is held together by…
lesson.bonding.q3: How many bonds can a single carbon atom form?
lesson.bonding.e1: Sodium transfers its outer electron to chlorine, producing Na⁺ and Cl⁻ held together by electrostatic attraction.
lesson.bonding.e2: Metallic bonding uses a sea of delocalised valence electrons shared by positive metal ions, which is why metals conduct.
lesson.bonding.e3: Carbon has four valence electrons and four vacancies in its second shell, so it forms four covalent bonds — the whole of organic chemistry depends on it.
lesson.balancing.title: Balancing Equations
lesson.balancing.summary: Conservation of mass in coefficient form. Balance confidently using algebra rather than trial and error.
lesson.balancing.e1: Four H on the left needs 2H₂, and two O needs one O₂, so the right becomes 2H₂O. Smallest whole numbers: 2 : 1 : 2.
lesson.balancing.e2: Six O atoms need 3O₂; that makes 6 O on the right, so 2Fe₂O₃, which then needs 4 Fe. Result 4 : 3 : 2.
lesson.balancing.q3: Why must equations be balanced at all?
lesson.balancing.e3: Conservation of mass. Every atom in the products must come from the reactants, so the coefficients are the only free variable.
lesson.reactionTypes.title: The Five Reaction Types
lesson.reactionTypes.summary: Synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement and combustion — and how to tell them apart on sight.
lesson.mole.title: Molar Mass and the Mole
lesson.mole.summary: The mole is a counting unit, not a mass. Connect particle number, grams and molar mass.
lesson.mole.q1: What is the molar mass of H₂O, in g/mol?
lesson.mole.q2: How many atoms are in one mole of any element?
lesson.mole.e2: That is Avogadro’s number, 6.02214076 × 10²³ particles per mole — atoms for an element, molecules for a compound, ions for a salt.
lesson.mole.q3: How many moles are in 44.0 g of CO₂?
lesson.solubility.title: Solubility Rules
lesson.solubility.summary: The rules that decide whether a salt dissolves. Learn the exceptions, not just the pattern.
lesson.solubility.q1: Which of these salts is always soluble?
lesson.solubility.e1: All nitrates dissolve, and so do all group-1 salts. BaSO₄, CaCO₃ and AgCl are the classic insoluble cases.
lesson.solubility.e2: Those three cations form chloride precipitates, which is exactly how the halide test for Cl⁻ works in the lab.
lesson.solubility.q3: A double-displacement reaction between two solutions is usually observable because…
lesson.solubility.e3: AgNO₃ + NaCl gives an immediate white AgCl cloud. The precipitate is the visible proof the reaction happened.
lesson.reactionTypes.q3: Which pattern always indicates a combustion?
lesson.reactionTypes.e1: Two simpler substances combine into one compound — that is the definition of a synthesis reaction.
lesson.reactionTypes.e2: One compound breaks into two simpler compounds. Quicklime production and baking soda in an oven both work this way.
lesson.reactionTypes.e3: Hydrocarbons burn completely to carbon dioxide and water. If O₂ is limited you get CO or soot instead.
